guideTitle: Best Streaming Mixers for Dual PC Streaming (2026)
metaTitle: Best Mixers for Dual PC Streaming 2026
metaDescription: Four streaming mixers that handle a gaming PC and a streaming PC compared on dual USB, routing, submixes, DSP and XLR preamps for clean stream audio.
expertTake: The MAONO G3 is the best mixer for dual PC streaming because its four faders, three submixes and dual PC routing let one surface govern both machines. The M-GAME RGB Dual USB is the value pick for a streamer who also feeds a console. Anyone running a single PC does not need a dual bus mixer and should buy a simpler box.
introParagraphs: A dual PC stream splits the work across two computers: one runs the game and the other encodes the broadcast. Audio has to cross that gap cleanly, which is where a mixer with two USB connections earns its keep.

The hard part is routing. The stream computer needs your microphone and game sound, you need to hear the game and chat in your headphones, and viewers should never hear their own echo. Mixers differ widely in how easily they let you build those separate mixes.

products.name: MAONO G3 gaming mixer, 4 faders, 3 submixes, dual PC setup
products.description:
The G3 is a desktop audio mixer and XLR interface built around the idea that every source should be reachable by a fader. Any audio source can be mapped to one of four faders, and three submixes let you build separate blends for yourself, your audience and a recording. The dual PC setup support means the game machine and the stream machine can each feed the box.

The flexibility comes with setup time. Mapping sources and building submixes takes an evening, the software is aimed at Windows, and a streamer who just wants a single mic box will find it overbuilt. Next to the Roland BRIDGE CAST ONE it offers more physical faders, while the Roland leans on hardware DSP and a simpler dual bus design.

Once routing is saved, daily use is fast. A typical dual PC arrangement sends game audio from the gaming computer, keeps chat in your headphones only and sends a clean blend of voice and game to the stream computer. Label the faders with tape, test the stream mix with a recording before going live and keep the software updated with the routing profile backed up. A good starting plan is fader one for the game, fader two for chat, fader three for music and fader four for the microphone monitor, then adjust to your own habits.
products.bestFor: Streamers who want hands on control of every source across two PCs.
pros: Four faders map to any audio source
Three submixes for stream, headphones and more
cons: Routing takes an evening to set up

products.name: BEACN Studio USB XLR interface with DSP and dual PC support
products.description:
The BEACN Studio concentrates on the voice. Its premium XLR to USB-C connection feeds an on board DSP chain with EQ, compression, an expander and gate, noise suppression and low frequency enhancement, so the processing happens in the box and not on either computer. The BEACN app manages where audio comes from and goes to and pairs with a separate BEACN mixer unit.

The tradeoff is that the Studio is an interface rather than a fader surface. Hands on level control comes from the companion hardware, so a streamer who wants faders on the desk needs more than the Studio alone. It is also worth noting that the app is where routing lives, so a streamer who dislikes software panels may find the workflow less direct than a mixer with a fader per source. Beside the MAONO G3 it puts quality of voice first and fader count second.

Because the processing lives in hardware, CPU load stays low on both machines, which matters when one PC is straining under a game and the other under an encode. Set the gate and compressor once with your microphone at its working distance and save the profile, since a changed room or microphone will need a quick retune. Keep the gate threshold just above the fan noise from your two computers, and listen to a recording with a game running so you hear the real conditions. Over time the Studio becomes a set and forget part of the chain.
products.bestFor: Streamers who want hardware voice processing off both computers.
pros: On board EQ, compression and gate
cons: Interface only, faders need extra hardware
Needs the BEACN app for routing

products.name: Roland BRIDGE CAST ONE dual bus streaming mixer

specList.label: Mixes
specList.value: Independent for you and your audience

products.description:
Roland's BRIDGE CAST ONE condenses the core of the BRIDGE CAST into a space saving design. A dual audio bus system creates independent mixes for you and your online audience, and a dedicated 32 bit hardware DSP keeps audio processing off your computer so games and encodes keep their resources.

Its compact body means fewer controls than the G3, and its dual bus design is simpler than three submixes. That simplicity helps a streamer who wants two clean mixes and nothing else, and it shortens the time between unboxing and a working stream. A smaller control surface also means fewer knobs to bump by accident during an intense game. For a dual PC setup, the separate buses make it straightforward to keep your own monitor mix apart from the stream mix.

The unit works best with a clear plan for audio flow. Decide which PC owns the game sound, route the microphone to the stream PC and test the mix with a recording. Keep the unit on a short USB cable and update the companion software when Roland releases changes. Because the processing is in hardware, your voice sounds the same whichever PC is under strain, which is a quiet but real advantage during a long session. Keep a backup of your settings after each change.
products.bestFor: Streamers who want two independent mixes in a compact, hardware processed box.
pros: Dual bus for separate stream and monitor mixes
cons: Fewer physical controls than the G3
Only two buses compared with three submixes

products.name: M-GAME RGB dual USB audio interface mixer with XLR and optical in
products.description:
The M-GAME RGB takes a practical approach to a two machine desk: dual USB connections let a gaming rig and a streaming rig both connect, and an optical input and console connection bring in more sources. An XLR input handles the microphone, and voice effects and customizable samples add personality.

It is a feature box rather than a studio tool, and the published details on preamp gain are limited. Next to the BEACN Studio it offers a broader connection list but less certainty about voice processing. The ability to assign images to samples and voice effects makes it fun for a stream with a strong brand.

Plan the cabling before you start, since a dual USB device with an optical input can create several routes. Label each cable at both ends and keep a note of which source feeds which input, so a swap during a busy stream does not send the game into the wrong channel. Test the console path separately from the PC paths, since optical audio needs the console's audio output set to the right format. Treat the sample pads as an extra, and keep clips short and quiet.
products.bestFor: Streamers with a game PC, a stream PC and a console on one desk.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A dual PC mixer needs one USB link to each computer, or one USB plus another path such as optical. Plug the cables into rear ports on each machine where possible, since a front panel hub can share bandwidth or lose power when a laptop sleeps. The MAONO G3 and M-GAME RGB advertise dual operation, and the BEACN Studio supports dual PC use through its app. A single USB mixer forces you to move audio through capture cards or virtual cables, which add latency and failure points.

You want one blend for the stream, a different one for your headphones and sometimes a third for a recording. The MAONO G3 provides three submixes and the Roland BRIDGE CAST ONE a dual bus. Without separate mixes, a loud alert in your ears reaches your audience too, and chat can leak into the broadcast.

Hardware DSP keeps compression and noise suppression off the computers. The Roland uses a 32 bit hardware DSP, and the BEACN Studio runs EQ, compression, gate and noise suppression on board. When two machines are already busy, offloading voice processing lowers the chance of dropped frames.

Faders let you turn the game down when a donation message arrives. The G3 has four mapped to any source, while the Studio is an interface and relies on extra hardware. If you rebalance live, faders save time; if you set levels once, an interface is enough.

The streamer's voice is the most important signal in the chain, and viewers will forgive a soft game image far sooner than a thin or noisy voice. The BEACN Studio and the G3 offer XLR inputs and processing, while the M-GAME gives an XLR input but little published detail. Check gain headroom if you use a quiet dynamic microphone.

If you also stream from a console, optical or line inputs matter, because many consoles send chat and game sound through different outputs and you will want both. A dual PC desk that grows to include a console quickly turns into a cabling puzzle, so a mixer with spare inputs saves a later purchase. The M-GAME lists optical in and a console connection, which the others do not emphasize. Plan the sources you need before you choose.

howWeEvaluated.title: Dual PC support
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked how each unit connects to two computers and keeps the audio paths separate. The MAONO G3 and M-GAME RGB advertise dual operation, and the BEACN Studio and Roland handle it through their apps and buses. We asked whether a single setup session would leave both machines working, or whether the unit assumed one computer and treated the second as an afterthought.

howWeEvaluated.title: Routing flexibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared submixes and buses, noting the G3's three submixes and the Roland's dual bus design. Independent mixes are the difference between a clean broadcast and one that carries your private alerts, so we rated flexibility highly, while noting that more routing options also mean more ways to misconfigure a stream.

howWeEvaluated.title: Voice processing
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at where processing happens and how complete it is, with the BEACN Studio's DSP chain and the Roland's hardware DSP leading. Processing in the box keeps your voice consistent whichever computer is under load, and it means a game update that spikes the CPU cannot suddenly change how your microphone sounds.

howWeEvaluated.title: Control surface
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed faders, knobs and software control, noting the G3's four faders versus the interface approach of the Studio. A streamer in the middle of a match has one hand on a mouse, so the speed of a control matters more than the number of controls, and a fader that can be nudged without looking beats a menu every time.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared price tiers, with the M-GAME at the lower end and the BEACN Studio and G3 higher. Value in a dual PC desk is partly the cost of what you avoid buying: a mixer that makes capture cards or virtual cables unnecessary effectively pays for itself, and we credited units that remove steps from the chain.

faq.q: Do I need a mixer for dual PC streaming?
faq.a: It simplifies audio routing between two computers. Without one you rely on capture cards and virtual cables, which add latency, extra software and more places for a stream to break. A hardware mixer with two USB links lets the gaming machine send game sound while the stream machine receives a finished blend of voice and game, with your own monitor mix kept separate.

faq.q: Which mixer is best for dual PC?
faq.a: The MAONO G3 is the best all round, with four faders, three submixes and dual PC support. The BEACN Studio is better when voice processing matters most, because EQ, compression and a gate run in the box. The Roland BRIDGE CAST ONE suits a streamer who wants two clean mixes in a compact unit and does not need many faders.

faq.q: Can I use one USB mixer?
faq.a: Yes, but you need a way to send game audio to the stream PC, usually by capture card or a virtual audio cable. That works for many streamers, though it concentrates load on one machine and can introduce sync drift between game audio and video. A mixer with two USB links avoids that by keeping the paths separate from the start.

It keeps processing off busy computers, which can prevent dropped frames. A gaming PC working hard on graphics and a stream PC working hard on an encode both have limited headroom, and moving compression and noise suppression into the mixer frees a little on each. The effect is subtle but valuable at the edge of what the machines can do.

faq.q: Can I connect a console too?
faq.a: The M-GAME lists optical and console connections, which is the most direct route for a console stream among these four. Other boards can take a console through a capture device or an analog line input, but check that the audio reaches the right bus before relying on it in a live show.

faq.q: Do I need an XLR microphone?
faq.a: XLR gives better quality, and all four mixers here accept one. A dynamic XLR microphone also rejects room and keyboard noise better than a typical USB desktop microphone, which matters on a desk crowded with two computers and their fans. Pair the microphone with a boom arm so it stays clear of the noisy hardware.
